**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on Surah 104 (al-Humaza), verse 1:**

[p. 243] **Surat al-Humaza: its purpose**

It is the declaration of the greatest, losing party, whom accumulation (*al-takathur*, ﴿the pursuit of more﴾) diverted, so that his loss became evident on the Day of the Striking Calamity (*al-Qari'a*), which brings low and raises up. Its name, *al-Humaza*, clearly indicates this. [It begins with] "In the name of Allah" (*bismillah*), to whom belongs perfect might, which is the just judgment; "the Most Merciful" (*al-Rahman*), whose manifest blessing encompasses both the miserly and the generous; "the Most Compassionate" (*al-Rahim*), who perfects His blessing upon whomever of His servants He wills, singling them out with grace.

* *

Because the surah of *al-Asr* distinguished between the saved and the two types of humanity and concluded with patience, a complete yearning arose for the attributes of the ruined. So He said, explaining the most misguided and wretched of them, whose harm is most severe to bear, so that the punishment prepared for him would be a consolation to the patient:

﴿Woe﴾, meaning a very great destruction, ﴿to every backbiter and slanderer﴾. *Humaza* refers to one for whom *hamz* has become a habit, because it is a fixed disposition in his nature. Likewise *lumaza*. *Al-hamz* is breaking, like crushing (*al-hazm*), and *al-lamz* is defamation. This is their original meaning. Then both were specialized to breaking people's honor and defaming them. Ibn Hisham said in *Tahdhib al-Sira*: *al-Humaza* is one who insults a man openly, makes faces at him and gestures at him with the eyes, while *al-Lumaza* is one who disparages people in secret. End of quote. Al-Baghawi said: The original sense of *al-hamz* is breaking and biting down on something violently. The form that indicates habitual action is the pattern *fu'ala* with *damma* and *fatha*, as one says *dhihka* for one who laughs much, until it becomes his habit and custom. The pattern *fi'la* with a sukun denotes the passive, the one who is mocked and slandered by people; it has also been read this way. It seems to be an allusion to one who deliberately sets out to do what he mocks and slanders, and thus becomes an object of ridicule, laughed at. And Allah knows best.

Imam Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: When the Exalted and Glorified said, ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [al-Asr: 2], He followed it with an example of [one who mentions his deficiency, his shortcoming, and his delusion, and who thinks perfection belongs to himself, to the point of defaming others, and who relies on the wealth he has gathered, supposing that it will make him immortal and save him. All of this is the very essence of deficiency, which is the condition of man, and which is mentioned in the surah before it]. So He said, ﴿Woe to every backbiter and slanderer.﴾ The surah therefore opens with mention of the punishment prepared for him as a recompense for his [against] *hamz* and *lamz*, by which he completes his envy. *Al-Humaza* is the one who censures and stabs, and *al-Lumaza* is similar. Then He, the Exalted, mentioned his wealth and his final abode by saying: ﴿He shall surely be thrown into the Crushing Fire (*al-Hutama*)﴾ [al-Humaza: 4], meaning he will be cast into the Fire as a recompense for his delusion and his slandering. End of quote.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 104, verse 2:

Since the one who commits belittling (al-naqisah) without any need compelling him to it is in a worse state, and since acquiring wealth (al-mutamawwil) was among them the thing that counts as gain, and they boast of gain and regard the one who attains it as among the people of high station, he said, restricting "kull" (every) by the description, clarifying the one who is utterly lost: ﴿who has gathered﴾. And since the unqualified form of gathering (al-jam') indicates abundance, the doubling of the consonant in its verb has come for Abu Ja'far, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i (intensive reading, jammaʿa). I took "khilt" (I thought) as an explicit statement of what was known by allusion and indication, showing that what is meant by it is the one who has made the world his greatest concern. The lightened reading (jama'a) is for the rest of them, relying on the basic meaning of the root, unlike "ʿaddada" (counted), for its bare form is used for what is small, and for this reason they agreed on doubling in it (ʿaddada). ﴿Wealth﴾, that is, great. He stressed the intended sense of abundance with his saying: ﴿and counted it﴾, that is, he made it such that when its number is wanted, time is lengthened in counting it and the counting becomes much; or he stored it and held it back, preparing for what will befall him in this passing world. He added to it another qualifier in describing his state, and so he said:

﴿Yaḥsabu﴾ (he thinks), owing to the weakness of his intellect, ﴿that his wealth﴾, that is, that which he has counted, ﴿has made him immortal﴾, that is, has brought him to the rank of immortality in this world. So he loves that wealth as one loves eternity. It is also possible that this is a metaphor (kināyah) for the fact that his conduct, by his immersion in sins, his turning away from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and his devotion to indulging in desires and fleeting worldly things, is the conduct of one who thinks he will never die. It is also possible that this is a new sentence (isti'nāf), and in it there is an allusion (ta'rīḍ) that only righteous deeds, which bring happiness in the Hereafter, grant true immortality. (p-246)

Since this supposing does not need a proof to refute it, given its extreme feebleness and the clarity of its weakness, He confined Himself regarding it to the particle of deterrence that encompasses every rebuke, saying: ﴿Nay﴾, meaning: what he supposes will not be, because he shall not have what others of his kind do not have, but he will die just as every living created being dies.

And since it was as if it were said: "So what will be done with him after death?", He said, swearing an oath, [indicating] by the lam that enters upon the verb for the oath: ﴿Surely he will be thrown﴾, meaning: he will surely be cast after his death with a casting that is light and very easy for any caster, as indicated by the expression "thrown" (al-nabdh) and the use of the passive voice, ﴿into the Huṭamah﴾, meaning the stratum of the Fire (ṭabaqah) that by its nature crushes (tuhashshamu) and breaks (tukassaru) with intensity and violence everything cast into it, so he will be among the greatest of losers. He expressed it with this name in contrast to the preparation with wealth that leads to contempt for creation. Al-Ustadh Abu al-Hasan al-Harali said: "For the meaning of what pertains to judgment, the Exalted names it by one of its names, such as Jahannam in what is a direct confrontation, and such as al-Huṭamah in what is a recompense, for the strength of subjugation and preparation by a number; and similarly for the rest of its names." And He, glorified and exalted, magnified its status by His saying:

﴿And what will make you know﴾, i.e., what could inform you, even through your own effort to seek knowledge and striving to comprehend it, along with your being the most knowledgeable of creation (p-247) ﴿what is al-Hutamah (the Crusher)?﴾, i.e., what is that fiery abyss, which was given this name for this property? For there is nothing in the existence you have witnessed that approximates it so as to serve as an example of it. Then he explained it with His saying:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 104, verse 6:

﴿The Fire of Allah﴾, i.e., the Greatest King, from whom the polytheists turned away to their partners. So the greatness of this Fire is from His greatness, and His retribution is from His vengeance. ﴿That is kindled﴾, i.e., whose kindling was brought into being and decreed to be by His kindling. And who is able to attempt what He has kindled? Thus this name remains constant for it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 104, verse 7:

When He described the one who slanders and defames (al-hamiz al-hazim), He then described the one who crushes (al-hatim), saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Which mounts over the hearts﴾. And since one cannot have knowledge of the states of a thing except one who is in front of it in knowledge, He said: ﴿rises up﴾ with a fierce rising ﴿upon the hearts﴾, the plural of fu'ad, which is the heart that nearly burns from the intensity of its ignition. It should have directed its fire toward the means of escape, but instead its rising upon it is by reaching its midst and enveloping it with a thorough enveloping. It is named thus because of the intensity with which it is kindled, and it is singled out for mention because it is the most delicate part of the body and the most sensitive to pain from the slightest harm, and because it is the source of corrupt beliefs and the mine of love of wealth, which is the source of corruption and misguidance, and from it proceed ugly deeds.

(p-248) Since being made aware of the heart is a likely cause of death, and in death there is relief from punishment, He indicated their abiding therein, and that they will neither die nor will the punishment be cut off from them. So He said, emphasizing because they [denied it]: ﴿Indeed it﴾, and He indicated their subjugation and defeat, so He said: ﴿upon them﴾, and He signified the ease with which they will be disposed of in punishment and the cutting off of hope for their deliverance by His words, expressing it with the form of the passive participle: ﴿closed over﴾, that is, sealed shut in utmost narrowness, from awsadtu al-bab (I closed the door), when I shut it tight.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 104, verse 9:

Since their custom in restraining a person from movement was to place a great wooden beam called the muqattara (stocks), in which there are rings through which the man is bound, so that after that its owner cannot move, he said, depicting their punishment by a state from the pronoun in "ʿalayhim" (upon them): ﴿In﴾ [i.e.,] being bound in ﴿columns﴾ (ʿamad, with two fatḥas or two ḍammas, the plural of ʿamud) ﴿stretched out﴾, i.e., extended, as if they were laid upon the ground, so they are in the utmost confinement, and the one bound by them cannot devise any kind of trick regarding his affair. This is an emphasis on their despair of escaping by being shut in after being locked up, and this is the greatest of torment and the severest of punishments, for its last part has returned to its first, and the joint of it has the tightest connection to what joins it. And God is the One who grants success to what is right, and to Him is the return and the final destination.
